20.prose:
He came down to the smell of porridge, paid two coppers for a bowl of it with brown bread, and ate by the hearth while the copper-haired innkeeper swept the floor around his boots. Nobody hurried him. When he shouldered up and asked the road east, she gave it plainly: "Through the gate, keep the river on your left, and it's Asterhall by nightfall if your legs hold."

His legs held. The east road ran along the river through country waking into its day—shepherds moving flocks off the wet grass, a lime-burner's smoke standing straight in the still air. At a ford crossing a carter raising water for his oxen nodded at him and went back to his ropes. Nothing on the road wanted anything from him, and he gave the road nothing back, just miles.

The land climbed gently through the afternoon, woods giving way to hedged fields, and near dusk Asterhall rose out of the plain—bigger than Glassmere by far, a real capital's outer sprawl of market gardens and tanneries wrapping walls that carried towers. Traffic thickened on the road: carts of kale, riders in good cloaks, a student in college grey arguing with her own satchel. A gate guard glanced at his scorched robes, at the staff, and waved him through with the boredom of a man who has seen ten thousand adventurers come home.

Inside, lamplighters were working the main street. He followed the crowd's grain and the painted signs, and found the Asterhall branch of the Adventurers' Guild as full evening settled—a broad stone hall, louder than Glassmere's receiving house, bright with lanterns. Adventurers crowded the benches, a board of postings stood along one wall, and a row of clerks worked the long counter at the far end.

A clerk with greying side-whiskers looked up from his ledger as Alaric came within reach of the counter, and put down his pen.

The Guild hall at Marrowbridge was smaller than Asterfall's — one long room, a notice board with a dozen slips, a stone-silled window looking out on the weir, and a desk behind which a broad woman with burn-scarred forearms was tallying something in a ledger. She looked up at the door's creak, took in his robes and staff, and set down her pen.

"Business?"

The slip came out of the pouch and crossed the counter. She flattened it under her palm, and the READY seal glowed faintly against the wood; her lips moved over the contract line, the four of four, the flats below Asterhall. She reached for a separate roll behind her, checked it against the slip, and nodded.

"Bog strider cull. Downstream branch took the posting." She drew a small tray from under the counter and counted copper onto it, coin by coin, her finger keeping the tally. "Ninety copper. The eel men will be glad — Toma's been losing weirs all season. He talk your ear off, did he? He does that."

She pushed the tray across and took the slip back, dipping a pen to mark the roll. "Contract's closed. Anything on the board takes your eye, it's Novice rank and under on the left side. We strike the day's listings at dark, mind, so read it before the lamps burn down."
